nodes.t: Tankers fuel five Mars ships for one window
nodes.d: In the months before one Mars launch window, tankers fill five or more Mars-bound Starships in Earth orbit, and the ships depart in that window.

nodes.t: Engine development time and cost cut
nodes.d: New liquid engines reach qualification with materially fewer hot-fire tests and redesign loops (for example >=30% fewer than the same organization's previous engine program of similar thrust class), with the saving attributed to predictive tools.

nodes.t: A new large engine flies four years after program start
nodes.d: A clean-sheet liquid rocket engine of at least 1 MN (about 225,000 lbf) thrust flies on an orbital-class launch within four years of its program start, as disclosed by the developer.

nodes.t: High-cadence instrumented reentry flights
nodes.d: A steady stream of instrumented hypersonic and orbital-reentry flights (Varda W-series, Talon-A, MACH-TB, Inversion Arc once flying, BOLT-class experiments) whose surface heating, pressure and in-depth TPS temperatures reach model builders beyond the vehicle operator.

nodes.t: Heat-shield margins from on-demand uncertainty analysis
nodes.d: Deterministic aerothermal factors and a separate material branch, combined by the traditional three-branch root-sum-square method, are replaced by a joint probabilistic budget that carries material, aerothermal and recession uncertainty across the full aeroshell to a reliability statement on bondline temperature…

nodes.t: Information-optimal ground and flight test design
nodes.d: Bayesian optimal experimental design and sequential model calibration choose arc-jet conditions, shock-tube shots and flight sensor placements.

nodes.t: On-demand airflow stability analysis for any vehicle
nodes.d: AI agents set up and run linear and nonlinear stability analyses (PSE, plane-marching PSE, resolvent/input-output, BiGlobal) on full 3D vehicle geometries with thermochemistry.

nodes.t: Math for finding hidden heat-shield damage
nodes.d: Uniqueness and stability theory, plus algorithms, for recovering hidden TPS defects (bondline disbonds, subsurface cracks, density variation) from surface thermography, ultrasound and strain data.

nodes.t: Certified simulation of thin upper-atmosphere flow
nodes.d: Hybrids of DSMC, Fokker-Planck and discrete-velocity methods, with proven consistency with the Boltzmann equation and quantified statistical error, used for high-altitude aerocapture passes, early-entry heating and plume backflow.

nodes.t: Error bounds for carrying ground-test heating data to flight
nodes.d: Rigorous or coverage-calibrated bounds on the error of aerothermal and material-response models when extrapolated from arc-jet and shock-tube conditions to flight, so that a probabilistic TPS margin can carry model-form error with stated coverage instead of a judgment factor.

nodes.t: Certified error bounds for hypersonic flow codes
nodes.d: Proven a-posteriori error bounds and formally verified kernels (positivity-preserving shock capturing, stiff finite-rate chemistry integrators, radiation-transport quadrature).

nodes.t: Damage-accumulation model for reusable ceramic tiles
nodes.d: A predictive model of tile cracking, edge chipping, bond fatigue and hot-gas ingress through gaps over repeated entries, tied to inspection data, so that operators can inspect by exception and set life limits per tile zone.

nodes.t: Predicting how heat-shield material burns away
nodes.d: Multiscale material response that goes from pore scale to volume average, with mathematically justified homogenization, calibrated permeability and pyrolysis kinetics, and criteria for spallation and char failure.

nodes.t: Heat-shield surface chemistry from first principles
nodes.d: Finite-rate oxidation, nitridation and catalytic-recombination models for carbon, SiC and silica-based (tile coating) surfaces, derived from quantum chemistry plus molecular-beam data, to replace tuned recession and catalycity parameters.

nodes.t: Predicting glowing-gas heating on the fastest entries
nodes.d: State-resolved excitation and dissociation kinetics (the CO 4th positive system in CO2 atmospheres; N and O VUV emission for Earth return), built from ab initio rates plus shock-tube data, that cut radiative-heating uncertainty from 30-100% to ~15-25%.

nodes.t: Better heating models where shock waves hit the vehicle
nodes.d: AI-derived RANS and wall-model closures (non-Boussinesq, variable turbulent Prandtl number, roughness and blowing) that predict separation extent and peak heating in shock-boundary-layer interactions (flaps, control surfaces, tile steps and gaps) to within ~+/-15-20% of DNS and experiment.

nodes.t: Predicting when hypersonic airflow turns turbulent
nodes.d: A validated model that predicts transition onset on 3D vehicles from the freestream disturbance environment, surface roughness and ablation blowing, to within ~+/-20% in transition Reynolds number, without per-vehicle tuning.

nodes.t: Predicting radio blackout during reentry
nodes.d: Coupled tools for nonequilibrium flowfield, electron density and full-wave electromagnetics that predict and minimize RF blackout through antenna placement, aft-side relay to constellations, and magnetic or electrostatic windows.

nodes.t: AI co-designs vehicle shape, entry path and heat shield
nodes.d: Multi-fidelity co-optimization of vehicle shape, entry trajectory and TPS layout, using AI-built surrogates (neural fields, reduced-order models) with validated or certified error bars.

nodes.t: Fleet-trained reentry heating model for one reusable vehicle
nodes.d: A physics-constrained model of reentry heating and TPS thermal response specific to one reusable vehicle family (Starship first), assimilated from 50 or more instrumented orbital reentries of that family (thermocouple and load-sensing tiles, imagery, trajectory reconstruction).

nodes.t: Probabilistic heat-shield sizing adopted in practice
nodes.d: A NASA program, an ESA mission or a commercial capsule maker formally sizes heat-shield thickness to a reliability target using joint probabilistic margins rather than stacked factors.

nodes.t: Validated models of braking with engines at supersonic speed
nodes.d: Predictive models of plume-shock interaction, aerodynamic forces and moments, and heating during supersonic retropropulsion (SRP) for 20-100 t Mars landers, reduced to control-oriented models with quantified uncertainty and accepted by a lander program.

nodes.t: AI-designed heat shields and hot structures
nodes.d: Computational design of ultra-high-temperature ceramics, high-entropy carbides and borides, ceramic-matrix composites and ablators, with predicted oxidation, ablation and fracture behaviour for reentry and hypersonic thermal protection systems (TPS).

nodes.t: Arc-jet test runs per year double
nodes.d: U.S. arc-jet facilities together complete at least twice as many heat-shield test runs a year as in 2026, from added facilities and from automated model change, instrumentation and turnaround between runs.

nodes.t: First aerocapture flight demonstration
nodes.d: A vehicle uses a single atmospheric pass to capture into orbit (an Earth demonstration), validating the guidance, aerothermal and model-correlation performance that a planetary flagship would need before relying on aerocapture.

nodes.t: Next large inflatable or folding heat shield flies
nodes.d: An orbital-entry flight of an inflatable (HIAD) or mechanically deployable (ADEPT) aeroshell of 10 m class or larger, the scale path toward the 16-18 m aeroshells studied for heavy Mars landers.

nodes.t: Rapidly reusable orbital heat shield (ship scale)
nodes.d: One Starship-class orbital vehicle reflies at least 5 times, with heat-shield turnaround under ~2 weeks and tile replacement limited to a small fraction per flight.

nodes.t: Flown heat shield sized with reduced, model-based margins
nodes.d: A flown reentry capsule or planetary probe whose TPS was sized by probabilistic, model-based margins and is at least ~10% thinner (or lighter) than the same operator's previous flown design for a comparable entry, with the reduction attributed to probabilistic sizing and flight data confirming the bondline predictions.

nodes.t: AI-designed heat-shield material flies
nodes.d: An AI-designed thermal-protection material, coating or ablator flies on a reentry vehicle.

nodes.t: Ground-validated design basis for 12-14 km/s Earth return
nodes.d: A validated aerothermal environment (radiative plus convective) and TPS response model (HEEET-class 3D woven material) for crewed Mars-return or other large-radius (nose radius above ~2-3 m) Earth entries at 12-14 km/s, where radiation dominates, with radiative uncertainty of 25% or less, accepted by a mission project.

nodes.t: First landing of 20 t or more on Mars
nodes.d: A Starship-class or other vehicle lands 20 t or more intact on Mars, demonstrating heavy Mars EDL: entry at ~6-7.5 km/s, aerobraking, then retropropulsive descent.

nodes.t: Point-to-point rocket cargo, repeated demonstration flights
nodes.d: At least 3 suborbital point-to-point flights deliver 30 t or more of cargo to remote landing sites, with the vehicle recovered, per the Space Force Point-to-Point Delivery (P2PD) concept.

nodes.t: Second heavy Mars lander lands within 1 km of the first
nodes.d: A second lander of 20 t or more, from the same launch window or a later one, lands intact on Mars within 1 km of an earlier lander, without disabling damage to it from plume or ejecta.

nodes.t: AI-designed heat-shield material in regular service
nodes.d: An AI-designed TPS material, coating or ablator (as defined in materials-tps-new-material-flight) is the baseline material for a primary heat-shield zone (forebody, nose or windward acreage) of an operational reentry vehicle and has flown at least 3 missions in that role.

nodes.t: People return from orbit on a reusable ship
nodes.d: A crew of at least two launches to orbit and returns to Earth aboard the ship of a fully reusable heavy launcher (Starship-class), which comes through entry on its reusable heat shield and lands for reuse, on a licensed flight.

nodes.t: Ship heat shield turned around in three days
nodes.d: One Starship-class ship reaches 20 orbital flights and, at least once, flies twice within 72 hours, with heat-shield inspection and tile work done at the launch site.

nodes.t: Crewed heat shield sized by probabilistic margins flies
nodes.d: A crewed reentry vehicle certified by NASA or another space agency flies a heat shield whose thickness was set to a reliability target with joint probabilistic margins, including a flight-calibrated model-form term, in place of stacked aerothermal factors.

nodes.t: First aerocapture into orbit around another planet
nodes.d: A funded spacecraft (science, relay or commercial) enters orbit around Mars, Venus or Titan with a single atmospheric pass as its planned orbit-insertion method.

nodes.t: Routine, cheap reentry: 50+ commercial returns a year
nodes.d: Commercial capsule returns (in-space manufacturing, defense hypersonic testbeds, cargo) exceed ~50 a year worldwide, and TPS is no longer a pacing or major cost item.

nodes.t: Aerocapture baselined for an outer-planet flagship
nodes.d: NASA or ESA baselines aerocapture for a Uranus, Neptune or Titan orbiter, cutting cruise time by years and shifting propellant mass to science.

nodes.t: Knowing how long perovskite cells last in orbit
nodes.d: Mechanistic, predictive models of perovskite and perovskite-tandem degradation (ion migration, phase segregation, proton and electron damage, ultraviolet, thermal cycling, self-healing) that map accelerated ground tests to on-orbit lifetime.

nodes.t: Predicting radiation errors in commercial AI chips
nodes.d: Hierarchical stochastic models that turn limited proton and heavy-ion beam data into mission-level rates of silent data corruption and functional interrupts for complex commercial processors, GPUs/TPUs and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) running real AI workloads.

nodes.t: Predictive simulation of large deployable structures
nodes.d: Validated models of deployment for 50 m to km structures: frictional contact and latching, stored-strain composite booms, tape-spring snap-through, membrane wrinkling and thermally induced vibration, where today's simulations lean on ground tests that gravity corrupts at scale.

nodes.t: Predictive two-phase cooling physics in microgravity
nodes.d: Validated mechanistic models of flow boiling, condensation, critical heat flux and flow-regime transitions in microgravity pumped loops and heat pipes, at the heat fluxes 100-250 kW compute satellites need.

nodes.t: Proven-stable power grids for big spacecraft and Moon bases
nodes.d: Large-signal stability and fault-protection proofs for high-voltage DC power systems feeding many constant-power loads (compute racks, electric-propulsion power processing units, electrolysis cells): Lyapunov, passivity or sum-of-squares certificates for the bus with its converters, filters and batteries…

nodes.t: AI-optimized radiators and heat transport
nodes.d: Coupled conduction-radiation-two-phase design optimization (panel topology, heat-pipe and loop layout, cold plates and heat spreading, view factors to Earth and arrays, micrometeoroid segmentation…

nodes.t: Proof agents verify space processors and chip logic
nodes.d: AI agents write the formal properties and proofs for space avionics hardware: RTL of radiation-tolerant processors and SoCs, FPGA designs re-verified after triple-modular-redundancy insertion, and error-correction and scrubbing logic…

nodes.t: Battery qualification without years of cycling
nodes.d: Physics-based and data-driven degradation models (solid-electrolyte-interphase growth, lithium plating, silicon-anode swelling, solid-state interfaces) that predict end-of-life capacity under low-Earth-orbit cycling from early-cycle data, with validated uncertainty.

nodes.t: Proven radiation-fault tolerance for orbital AI
nodes.d: Machine-checked proofs that fault-tolerance layers (error-correcting codes, memory scrubbing, checkpointing, algorithm-based fault tolerance for matrix operations, voting logic) bound the probability of undetected errors under a stated radiation fault model.

nodes.t: Second-generation fission power designs
nodes.d: AI multiphysics optimization of reactor, shield, Brayton converter, radiator and lander integration for follow-on fission systems (lower kg/kWe at 100 kWe-plus, Mars or nuclear-electric variants) after the first unit's design is frozen.

nodes.t: 100-kW-class deployable radiators fly on compute satellites
nodes.d: First flights of deployable liquid or two-phase radiators rejecting 100-250 kW per spacecraft (SpaceX Starmind: the June 2026 AI1 spec had 110 m2 at Musk's ~1,400 W/m2 for 150 kW; the Aug-Sep 2026 revision runs 175 kW average / 250 kW peak inside a filed radiator envelope under 200 m2…

nodes.t: AI chips and memory qualified to run hot in orbit
nodes.d: Accelerator logic and HBM stacks are shown, by accelerated life tests, physics-of-failure models (electromigration, gate-oxide breakdown, bias-temperature instability, HBM retention and refresh, solder and through-silicon-via fatigue, combined with dose) and on-orbit telemetry…

nodes.t: Lightweight solar arrays at compute-constellation volume
nodes.d: Flexible or roll-out arrays at array-level specific power of roughly 125-140 W/kg or better (for example silicon at ~250 W/m2 on ~1.8-2 kg/m2 blankets) built at compute-constellation volume, hundreds of thousands of m2 a year.

nodes.t: AI-designed radiation-tolerant space processor
nodes.d: Agentic EDA designs and formally verifies a radiation-tolerant processor, SoC or AI accelerator designed for orbit (error correction, upset-aware layout, selective redundancy); it is taped out and heavy-ion tested, with design and verification credited mainly to agentic EDA.

nodes.t: Model-qualified perovskite tandem proves itself in orbit
nodes.d: A perovskite tandem (on silicon, CIGS or III-V) whose composition and encapsulation were optimized with validated degradation models completes at least one year in low Earth orbit with under 10% relative power loss, as predicted.

nodes.t: Radiation-robust high-voltage power electronics
nodes.d: SiC power MOSFETs (600-1,200 V class) redesigned to run near rated voltage in space, whether by empirical hardening or with a mechanism-level model of heavy-ion single-event burnout and leakage degradation.

nodes.t: Lightweight 600 K radiators qualified for fission power
nodes.d: Titanium-water or cesium-titanium heat-pipe radiator panels near 3 kg/m2 rejecting the ~230-300 kW of waste heat from a 100 kWe Brayton system, qualified for launch vibration, freeze-thaw and ~10 years of lunar micrometeoroid exposure.

nodes.t: Ultralight radiators in serial production
nodes.d: Two-phase or oscillating-heat-pipe deployable radiators at or below 2.5 kg/m2 planform, running at ~370 K chip temperature, built at Starlink-like volume (thousands of m2 per month).

nodes.t: A 1,000 m2-class solar sail flies
nodes.d: A solar sail of at least ~1,000 m2 (NASA's follow-on boom class targets up to 2,000 m2) flies, qualified substantially by validated deployment simulation plus subscale tests.

nodes.t: Commercial AI chips running in orbit at scale
nodes.d: Operational orbital AI compute (satellites or clusters of 100 kW class or more with paying customers) on commercial accelerators.

nodes.t: Tight-formation compute clusters operate in orbit
nodes.d: Operational clusters of about 10 or more compute satellites holding station within a few hundred metres (inside ~750 m), linked by terabit-class optical crosslinks (~10 Tbps per cluster per SpaceX), running models too large for one satellite.

nodes.t: Perovskite arrays power operational satellites
nodes.d: Perovskite-based (tandem or thin-film) arrays serve as primary power on operational spacecraft, for example lightweight arrays for compute or broadband constellations.

nodes.t: 100 kW-per-tonne compute satellites in serial production
nodes.d: Compute satellites at ~100 kW/t (versus AI1's ~70 kW/t design point and a Starlink V3-like ~11 kW/t) built at hundreds to thousands per year.

nodes.t: Megawatt-class compute satellites fly
nodes.d: A compute satellite with at least 1 MW of solar power flies and operates.

nodes.t: A 100 kW-electric fission reactor operating on the Moon
nodes.d: A fission surface power system delivering at least 100 kWe operates on the lunar surface (one-year demonstration followed by nine operational years in NASA's plan).

nodes.t: 100 MW of orbital compute outside dawn-dusk orbits
nodes.d: At least 100 MW of compute operates in orbits other than dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, such as inclined low orbits, medium Earth orbit or high Earth orbit.

nodes.t: Kilometre-scale monolithic structure in orbit
nodes.d: A single connected structure at least 1 km across (solar-radiator plane for GW compute, space solar power array or large antenna) deployed or assembled in orbit.

nodes.t: 1 GW of compute operating in orbit
nodes.d: Cumulative at least 1 GW of compute power in orbit, counted at nameplate (peak) rating: about 4,000 Starmind-class satellites at 250 kW peak (about 5,700 at the 175 kW average rating).

nodes.t: A step change in spacecraft power per kilogram
nodes.d: A fleet-level gain of 30% or more in power-system specific power (W/kg of arrays, storage and power electronics) on new spacecraft, attributable to new materials: perovskite or thin-film PV, high-voltage radiation-robust wide-bandgap electronics, higher-energy cells.

nodes.t: A large AI model is trained in orbit
nodes.d: An AI lab releases or deploys a model whose main training run, at least 1e26 FLOP, ran mainly on orbital compute.

nodes.t: 10 GW of compute operating in orbit
nodes.d: Orbital data centers with at least 10 GW of combined power operate in orbit, about 40,000 satellites at 250 kW or fewer larger ones.

nodes.t: Reaction networks that never lose an ingredient
nodes.d: Family 149 claims boundedness and persistence for every finite weakly reversible mass-action network with positive constant rates: each solution from a strictly positive start stays between epsilon and 1/epsilon for all time, with epsilon depending on network…

nodes.t: Rigorous theory of frictional contact
nodes.d: Existence, uniqueness or explicit selection rules for rigid and near-rigid bodies with many frictional contacts and impacts (the Painleve paradox regime), plus convergence proofs and rates for the time-stepping schemes that robot simulators actually use.

nodes.t: Reliable equations for flowing lunar soil
nodes.d: Prove well-posedness (or pinpoint ill-posedness and its minimal regularization) for continuum models of dense granular flow such as mu(I) rheology and nonlocal granular-fluidity models, so excavation, conveying…

nodes.t: Known limits for robot fleet scheduling
nodes.d: Hardness and optimality results tell surface-ops planners which multi-robot task-allocation, scheduling, partitioning and depot-siting problems can be solved near-optimally and which cannot, so effort moves to problem structure, exact solvers on small instances and heuristics.

nodes.t: Mission planners that are correct by design
nodes.d: Planners, schedulers and fault responses generated automatically from temporal-logic specifications (reactive synthesis, energy/mean-payoff games, probabilistic model checking) at the scale of real surface operations, each shipped with a proof that the plan meets the spec under the modeled environment.

nodes.t: Honest reliability numbers for life support
nodes.d: System-of-systems reliability, sparing and crew-maintenance models for regenerative life support with Bayesian uncertainty from ISS failure history: the analysis that decides how many tonnes of spares a Mars crew carries and how much crew time maintenance eats.

nodes.t: Fast, trustworthy models of oxygen reactors
nodes.d: Reduced-order multiphysics models (electrochemistry, melt flow and heat transfer, gas evolution, composition drift) of molten-regolith electrolysis, carbothermal and solid-oxide reactors, with error bounds, used for model-predictive control, optimal test design and scale-up decisions.

nodes.t: Contact simulators with error bars
nodes.d: Physics engines for grasping, latching, digging and assembly that carry proven convergence and computable error bounds for stated friction and compliance parameters, so a simulation run can count as verification evidence instead of a physical test.

nodes.t: Knowing what is worth making in orbit
nodes.d: Validated models of microgravity processing (ZBLAN fiber crystallization; vapor-phase growth of GaN, SiC, AlN and diamond; pharmaceutical crystallization) that quantify the quality gain over the best terrestrial processes and predict which products justify launch and return.

nodes.t: Biological life-support loops with stability guarantees
nodes.d: Multi-compartment models of bioregenerative life support (bacteria, algae, higher plants, crew) with certified stability and recovery margins, and controllers designed against those margins.

nodes.t: Validated models of digging icy regolith
nodes.d: Calibrated continuum-plus-DEM models (well-posed where theory allows, empirically regularized otherwise) of excavation, conveying and trafficability for polar regolith, including ice-cemented and vapor-deposited ice forms, predictive enough to size excavators and water-extraction feeders.

nodes.t: Predicting how lander exhaust erodes the surface
nodes.d: Validated models of how lander engine plumes erode regolith (rarefied-to-continuum gas flow, granular ejecta, cratering), used to set landing-site and engine-placement requirements.

nodes.t: Anodes that survive molten regolith
nodes.d: Discovery and life prediction of inert anode and crucible materials for oxygen-evolving electrolysis of molten regolith at ~1,600 C, the component that limits molten-regolith-electrolysis plant life.

nodes.t: Narrower uncertainty on crew radiation risk
nodes.d: Mechanistic radiobiology models (high-LET track structure, non-targeted effects, dose-rate) that shrink the uncertainty on cancer and cardiovascular risk per unit dose for Moon and Mars crews.

nodes.t: Crew-side fault diagnosis without Mission Control
nodes.d: Onboard diagnosis and repair guidance for habitats, life support and crew medicine that a crew 3-22 light-minutes (one way) from Earth can trust: model-based reasoning and AI assistants whose conclusions are cross-checked against verified system models.

nodes.t: Proof-checked autonomy software for lunar robots
nodes.d: Flight software for uncrewed rovers, excavators and other robotic surface assets whose planner, fault responses and safety monitors ship with machine-checked proofs: a synthesized planner plus a runtime-assurance wrapper around learned perception, produced by AI agents at a cost a commercial lunar company can afford.

nodes.t: Reliable recipes for sintering regolith
nodes.d: Process windows and closed-loop control for microwave, solar or laser sintering and melting of regolith into landing pads, roads and blast berms, avoiding thermal-stress cracking in lunar thermal extremes.

nodes.t: Robot assembly skills with proven safety envelopes
nodes.d: Learned or optimized manipulation skills (connector mating, truss and solar-array assembly, cable routing, refueling interfaces) wrapped in certified contact simulation and runtime assurance, so qualification can lean on analysis rather than exhaustive physical testing.

nodes.t: Design excavators from models, not guesses
nodes.d: Model-based sizing and design optimization of excavators, conveyors and ice-processing feeders for polar regolith, replacing much of today's build-and-dig-in-simulant iteration.

nodes.t: First measurements of how hard polar ice is to dig
nodes.d: In-situ geotechnical and volatile data from lunar south-pole regolith (VIPER, CLPS drills, Chang'e-7, LUPEX, Moon Base Phase 1 rovers): the physical data gate for every excavation and water-extraction model.

nodes.t: First oxygen made on the Moon
nodes.d: A flight demonstration that extracts at least 1 g of oxygen from lunar regolith on the surface (grams to kilograms), by carbothermal reduction, molten-regolith electrolysis, hydrogen reduction or another route.

nodes.t: A lunar robot operates with proof-checked autonomy
nodes.d: An uncrewed rover, excavator or other robotic surface asset operates on the Moon using autonomy software whose planner and safety monitors carry machine-checked proofs.

nodes.t: Long closed life-support test run by certified control
nodes.d: A ground test of 180+ days in which a bioregenerative or hybrid life-support loop runs under model-based control with stability certificates, at 95% or more material closure (food, O2, water).

nodes.t: Robotic assembly in space with certified skills
nodes.d: An on-orbit or lunar-surface demonstration of multi-step robotic assembly (structure, array or connector mating) using learned or optimized skills qualified mainly by certified simulation plus runtime assurance.

nodes.t: Kilogram-per-hour propellant production on Mars
nodes.d: A MOMS-class solid-oxide unit (1-3 kg O2/h plus methane) operating on Mars, 80-250x MOXIE's peak rate.

nodes.t: First robot-built landing pad or blast berm on the Moon
nodes.d: Autonomous machines build a landing pad or blast berm of tens of square meters or more from local regolith on the Moon (sintered, melted or 3D-printed), using process windows from auton-sinter-process-control.

nodes.t: AI-found air-scrubber or fuel-plant material qualified
nodes.d: A carbon-dioxide sorbent, a Sabatier or reverse-water-gas-shift catalyst, or a solid-oxide electrolysis electrode found by machine-learned atomistic screening and autonomous labs passes a space-relevant qualification test (thousands of hours of cycling with humidity and trace contaminants, vibration…

nodes.t: AI plans rover operations, machines check the plans
nodes.d: Routine use of AI agents to plan multi-sol rover traverses and multi-robot surface activities, with automated simulation and formal checks replacing most human plan review.

nodes.t: Heavy cargo landed on the Moon
nodes.d: A refueled Starship or Blue Moon Mk2 cargo lander delivers at least 15 t of useful payload to the lunar south-pole region in one landing.

nodes.t: Lunar base runs itself between crew visits
nodes.d: Robots, LTVs and base systems operate, maintain and resupply lunar base elements autonomously for months between crewed landings, with Earth supervising rather than commanding.

nodes.t: Moon Base Phase 2 infrastructure on the surface
nodes.d: At one south-polar site, the following are landed and operating: night-surviving surface power of tens of kW (ridge-site solar with storage, or fission), surface communications, LTVs and a logistics cache, plus at least one semi-habitable element.

nodes.t: Products made in orbit sold at recurring volume
nodes.d: In-space-manufactured semiconductor substrates or crystals, or ZBLAN fiber, sold commercially at recurring volume, with quality advantages predicted by validated models.

nodes.t: Robots prepare a Mars landing site and power
nodes.d: Robots delivered by a 20 t-class Mars landing deploy at least 100 kW of power, survey and dig for ice, and prepare a site for later ships, working through at least one Mars season under Earth supervision with a one-way light time of 3-22 minutes.

nodes.t: Tonne-per-year lunar oxygen plant
nodes.d: An operational lunar oxygen plant producing at least ~1 t/yr toward a 10 t/yr pilot scale, feeding life support and lander propellant.

nodes.t: Ten heavy cargo landings on the Moon in one year
nodes.d: Ten or more cargo landings of at least 10 t each reach the lunar surface in one calendar year, from Starship, Blue Moon or other heavy landers.

nodes.t: First water mined from lunar polar ice
nodes.d: A pilot plant digs ice-bearing regolith in or beside a permanently shadowed crater at the lunar south pole and extracts at least 1 t of water in one campaign, measured and stored.

nodes.t: Mars-class closed-loop life support, demonstrated
nodes.d: Regenerative ECLSS with at least 98% water recovery, 75%+ oxygen recovery and demonstrated reliability good enough for a ~1,000-day Mars mission, flown on ISS, a commercial station or a lunar habitat.

nodes.t: Crops grown through repeated harvests on the Moon
nodes.d: A pressurized plant module at a lunar base completes at least three successive harvests of a food crop under model-based stability control, tended by crew or robots.

nodes.t: Starship-scale propellant plant on Mars
nodes.d: Mars ISRU producing on the order of 1,000 t of methane and oxygen per return flight: about 65 kg O2/h over ~500 days, roughly 5,000x MOXIE's peak rate, plus water-ice mining and order-1-MW continuous power (general estimates).

nodes.t: Severalfold more robot work per operator
nodes.d: Useful surface work (km driven, kg excavated, tasks completed) per ground-operator hour rises severalfold (3-10x, judgment) versus 2025 practice on lunar or Mars surface robots.

nodes.t: Crews stay on the Moon for 90 days or more
nodes.d: A crew of two or more lives at a lunar surface base for 90 days or longer in one stay, and the base runs itself between crews.

nodes.t: A hundred robots work on the Moon at once
nodes.d: At least 100 robots of 20 kg or more (rovers, excavators, manipulators or humanoid-class machines) do excavation, hauling, construction or maintenance on the lunar surface at the same time, survive the lunar night, and are supervised by a ground team of fewer than 50 people using AI planning and machine-checked plans.

nodes.t: Mars outpost logistics cut by local resources and recycling
nodes.d: Validated ISRU, closed-loop life support and robot-first precursors reduce Earth-supplied mass for a first Mars outpost materially.

nodes.t: Lunar oxygen fuels landers at 10 t a year
nodes.d: A second-generation lunar plant makes oxygen at an annualized 10 t a year or more, from regolith or from polar ice, and at least 1 t of it is liquefied and transferred into a lander or depot as propellant.

nodes.t: NASA science budget held near its 2026 level
nodes.d: Exogenous programmatic gate: Congress again rejects the proposed cut to NASA's Science Mission Directorate (-47% in the FY2027 request) and funds HWO pre-formulation and the Explorer lines near FY2026 levels (HWO $150M).

nodes.t: Warp drives: sharp no-go theorems
nodes.d: Theorems stating, for every metric in a broad class, how much negative energy a 'warp' or 'propellantless' spacetime needs, or how much positive mass a positive-energy version must carry.

nodes.t: Beyond-Einstein gravity made simulable
nodes.d: Proving which modified-gravity theories have a well-posed initial-value problem, so black-hole mergers can be simulated and turned into templates, or proving they do not.

nodes.t: Black-hole foundations settled and checked
nodes.d: Independent experts confirm the 2026 wave of mathematical general relativity: nonlinear stability of Kerr black holes across the full subextremal range (human preprints, Jun and Sep 2026), the AI-claimed strong cosmic censorship near Kerr (family 264) and the AI-claimed spacetime Penrose inequalities (family 260).

nodes.t: Hard limits on negative energy from quantum fields
nodes.d: Quantum energy inequalities cap how much negative energy a quantum field can hold and for how long.

nodes.t: Proven limits for starlight suppression
nodes.d: Sharp, provable bounds on how much planet light any coronagraph can deliver at a given inner working angle, bandwidth and 1e-10 contrast for HWO's candidate apertures (on-axis segmented versus off-axis), plus designs that approach them.

nodes.t: What space interferometry can prove about black holes
nodes.d: Identifiability and stability theorems for sparse-aperture imaging: which Earth-space baselines (lengths, orientations, frequencies) uniquely determine a black hole's photon-ring diameter and shape, and hence its spin and the Kerr hypothesis, despite unknown plasma emission and station gain errors.

nodes.t: Cosmology inference that knows its own errors
nodes.d: Simulation-based inference, emulators and covariance estimates with proven calibration and error bounds, so Stage-IV surveys (DESI, Euclid, Rubin, Roman) can separate new physics from analysis artefacts with far fewer expensive simulations.

nodes.t: Earth-observation retrievals with honest error bars
nodes.d: Identifiability limits and analysis-backed, validated uncertainty for the inverse problems that turn Earth-observation measurements into numbers people act on: methane and CO2 point-source emission rates from shortwave-infrared and hyperspectral imagers…

nodes.t: 3D Sun-to-Earth reconstructions with guarantees
nodes.d: Uniqueness and stability theory, plus certified algorithms, for reconstructing the 3D corona and solar wind (density and magnetic structure) from a few viewpoints and polarized light, a problem now solved with ad hoc regularization.

nodes.t: Exoplanet atmosphere readings with honest error bars
nodes.d: Theorems and certified tools stating which molecules, abundances and temperature structures a given spectrum can and cannot determine (identifiability), plus retrieval methods robust to wrong one-dimensional model assumptions.

nodes.t: Merger simulations precise enough for LISA's loudest signals
nodes.d: LISA will see massive black-hole mergers at signal-to-noise ratios in the hundreds to thousands, where waveform error dominates the error budget.

nodes.t: LISA's hardest waveforms computed for spinning black holes
nodes.d: Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (a stellar-mass black hole spiraling ~1e5 orbits into a massive one) can only be decoded if the phase is modeled to better than about a radian over the whole signal.

nodes.t: Is dark energy changing? A decisive answer
nodes.d: Confirmation at >=5 sigma of DESI's hint that dark energy evolves, or the preference falling below ~2-3 sigma, using final DESI data combined with Euclid, Rubin, Roman and CMB data.

nodes.t: Coronal heating: an AI-built model passes a blind test
nodes.d: A predictive model of coronal heating and solar-wind acceleration, built by AI from Parker Solar Probe, Solar Orbiter and PUNCH data, makes a discriminating quantitative prediction (one on which the leading mechanisms, waves and turbulence versus small-scale reconnection and switchbacks…

nodes.t: Molecular fingerprints good enough for biosignature claims
nodes.d: Accurate line lists, pressure broadening and collision-induced absorption for biosignature and false-positive molecules (DMS, DMDS, CH3Cl, N2O, PH3, O2-O2 and others) over the needed temperatures, computed by AI-driven quantum chemistry and validated in the laboratory.

nodes.t: Knowing when 'signs of life' are not life
nodes.d: Predictive photochemistry, geochemistry and 3D climate models that list the non-biological routes to O2, O3, CH4 with CO2, DMS and other biosignatures for a given star and planet, with probabilities attached.

nodes.t: Earth-mass planet found in a Sun-like star's habitable zone
nodes.d: A planet under 2 Earth masses in the habitable zone of a nearby G or K dwarf is detected by radial velocity at 3 sigma or better, and the detection survives independent re-analysis.

nodes.t: AI mines the space-science archive at scale
nodes.d: AI systems that pose and answer research questions against archival mission data (JWST, Hubble, Gaia, TESS, Fermi, Parker Solar Probe, SDO), building models, running analyses and drafting results, with humans choosing problems and auditing.

nodes.t: Extraordinary claims audited in weeks
nodes.d: Independent AI re-analyses and certified checks of extraordinary claims (biosignatures, dark-energy anomalies, new-physics hints, exotic-propulsion metrics) published within weeks, with interval-certified or Lean-checked components where possible.

nodes.t: Lightsails proven to ride the beam
nodes.d: Sail shapes and metasurface designs with proven passive stability under laser propulsion (no tumbling or sliding off the beam) plus thermal and structural margins: the math-and-design half of beamed interstellar-precursor propulsion, the physics-allowed alternative to warp concepts.

nodes.t: Quantum sensors designed against full error budgets
nodes.d: AI-derived systematic-error models (relativistic time transfer, magnetic and gravity-gradient effects, wavefront aberrations) and provably robust quantum-control sequences for space clocks and atom interferometers.

nodes.t: Sun-watching constellations designed for best coverage
nodes.d: Choosing how many spacecraft, where (L1, L4/L5, polar, inner heliosphere) and what they measure, by proving which configurations make the 3D reconstruction unique and stable, instead of choosing by heritage and intuition.

nodes.t: Picometer-stable telescopes with guaranteed control
nodes.d: Wavefront sensing-and-control loops with proven convergence and robustness bounds against thermal and vibration disturbances, co-designed with the error budget, keeping contrast drift below ~1e-11 over hours-long exposures.

nodes.t: Habitable Worlds Observatory design closed by AI modeling
nodes.d: End-to-end integrated models (structure, thermal, optics, coronagraph, retrieval, survey yield) run and optimized by AI and used to freeze HWO's aperture, coronagraph type, wavelength range and stability requirements with quantified science yield.

nodes.t: Spacecraft send answers, not raw data, with error bounds
nodes.d: A science mission (smallsat, hosted payload or Explorer-class; new, or by software upload to an operating spacecraft) runs onboard inference that turns raw instrument data into science products (event detections, classifications, spectral fits…

nodes.t: LISA analysis stack passes its accuracy tests
nodes.d: End-to-end validation in LISA mock-data challenges: waveform models (post-adiabatic self-force inspirals, NR-calibrated mergers) plus the 'global fit' that separates tens of thousands of overlapping signals, shown to recover injected parameters without bias at realistic signal strengths.

nodes.t: AI-co-designed quantum sensor flies
nodes.d: A space atom-interferometer gravity gradiometer or next-generation clock whose design and control were materially derived with AI demonstrates its predicted sensitivity in orbit.

nodes.t: Laser-propelled gram-scale sail demonstrated
nodes.d: Demonstration of stable laser-driven propulsion of a gram-scale sail over meters or more, in a ground vacuum facility or in free (suborbital or orbital) flight.

nodes.t: Next-generation dark-energy survey data in hand
nodes.d: The data supply behind the dark-energy question: DESI's final BAO analyses and Euclid's first cosmology release are public, with early Rubin and Roman survey data arriving.

nodes.t: A privately funded space telescope returns data
nodes.d: A philanthropically or commercially funded space telescope of 1 m aperture class or larger, built outside agency selection and appropriations, returns science data.

nodes.t: Satellite methane data used as compliance evidence
nodes.d: A regulator, accredited verifier or treaty body uses satellite emission-rate quantification (methane super-emitters, CO2 point sources), with its stated uncertainty, as evidence in a compliance determination, a penalty, a verified correction to reported company or national emissions…

nodes.t: Science mission built to downlink onboard answers flies
nodes.d: A science mission selected after 2028 puts onboard science products with certified error bounds into its requirements, so its downlink and ground segment are sized for answers.

nodes.t: Exoplanet atmosphere census with honest error bars
nodes.d: ESA's ARIEL, or another survey of hundreds of exoplanet atmospheres, publishes population results with per-planet identifiability statements: which molecules and temperature structures each spectrum determines and which it cannot.

nodes.t: First space mission to sharpen black-hole images flies
nodes.d: A BHEX-class satellite links with ground telescopes to measure a black hole's photon ring, producing the sharpest images in astronomy.

nodes.t: A second privately funded space telescope returns data
nodes.d: A philanthropically or commercially funded space telescope of 1 m aperture class or larger, other than Lazuli and started after it, returns science data.

nodes.t: LISA launches
nodes.d: ESA's Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, three spacecraft 2.5 million km apart, launches toward its orbit around the Sun.

nodes.t: Sun-watching fleet built to map the solar wind in 3D flies
nodes.d: A multi-spacecraft heliophysics or space-weather mission (smallsats at several viewpoints, or L4/L5 plus polar) whose number, placement and instruments were chosen by reconstruction-uniqueness analysis launches and returns 3D coronal or solar-wind reconstructions with stated uncertainty.

nodes.t: LISA does precision strong-gravity science from day one
nodes.d: When LISA flies, its first-year data yield unbiased black-hole masses and spins, extreme-mass-ratio tests of the Kerr metric and bounds on beyond-Einstein theories, because the theory work was finished years before launch instead of during operations.

nodes.t: No-go theorems redirect breakthrough-propulsion money
nodes.d: Sharp, audited no-go results move the small pool of breakthrough-propulsion funding and attention away from warp and reactionless concepts toward physics-allowed frontiers (fusion, beamed sails).

nodes.t: More science per mission dollar
nodes.d: With analysis, theory and modeling nearly free, the science extracted from each flown observatory rises sharply; photons, downlink and mission count become the bottleneck of space science.

nodes.t: Space science shifts money from analysis to photons
nodes.d: Agencies and decadal surveys rebalance toward more data-collecting missions (small satellites, rideshares, probes) and laboratory data, because AI makes analysis and theory cheap.

nodes.t: Satellite methane data routinely correct reported emissions
nodes.d: Satellite emission-rate quantification with stated uncertainty becomes a standard verification input under at least one major regime: EU Methane Regulation operator reporting, importer equivalence or methane-intensity checks; a national regulator's penalty or super-emitter program…

nodes.t: Proven bounds on how Earth-Moon trajectories drift
nodes.d: Computer-assisted proofs, with explicit constants, of transport, diffusion and escape-time bounds in realistic restricted and full three- and four-body models (Earth-Moon CR3BP and bicircular models…

nodes.t: Long-term orbit stability proven for realistic systems
nodes.d: Quantitative KAM, Nekhoroshev and Arnold-diffusion theorems for realistic n-body parameters: rigorous lower bounds on stability times and upper bounds on diffusion rates for the solar system, resonant asteroid and cislunar orbits, and long-lived constellation dynamics.

nodes.t: Tracking objects in chaotic Earth-Moon space
nodes.d: Orbit determination, initial orbit determination, sensor tasking and uncertainty propagation for non-Keplerian cislunar orbits (NRHO, DRO, L1/L2 halos, transfers) from sparse optical data, with proven consistency and custody guarantees.

nodes.t: Provably safe maneuver-coordination rules
nodes.d: Coordination protocols for independently operated autonomous fleets (right-of-way rules, maneuver-intent exchange, behaviour under communication loss) with machine-checked proofs that compliant fleets never maneuver into each other, plus game-theoretic analysis of non-cooperating operators.

nodes.t: Certified merging of tracks from many sensors
nodes.d: Methods that fuse detections from hundreds to thousands of space-based sensors into tracks of many objects at once, with certified optimality gaps on the data-association step (which detection belongs to which object), consistent covariances under sensor bias and dropouts…

nodes.t: Navigation filters with proven error bounds
nodes.d: Estimators for autonomous navigation (optical and terrain-relative, X-ray pulsar, GNSS at lunar distance, crosslink ranging) with machine-checked consistency and integrity bounds (protection levels), including non-Gaussian and sensor-fault cases.

nodes.t: Certified collision-probability math
nodes.d: Fast methods that propagate orbit uncertainty that has become non-Gaussian (curved, skewed, multimodal) and compute probability of collision (Pc) with rigorous error bounds, replacing the 2D Gaussian Pc shortcut where it fails.

nodes.t: Sun-to-Earth ensemble forecasting with honest uncertainty
nodes.d: Coupled data assimilation from the Sun (SDO imagery and magnetograms, coronagraphs) through the solar wind (SOLAR-1 at L1) to the magnetosphere, ionosphere and thermosphere, producing ensemble forecasts with calibrated probabilities rather than single deterministic runs…

nodes.t: Certified map of stable Earth-Moon orbits
nodes.d: Validated (interval or Taylor-model) certified regions where lunar frozen orbits, DROs and stable resonant orbits stay bounded for 10-100 years without control, plus, for unstable halo/NRHO families, certified controlled envelopes and station-keeping delta-v budgets for stated navigation and maneuver-execution errors.

nodes.t: Debris-cascade tipping-point models with error bars
nodes.d: Long-term debris-environment models (source-sink and Monte Carlo) with proven stability thresholds (when runaway collisional growth starts) and honest uncertainty from fragmentation physics and compliance assumptions.

nodes.t: Upper-atmosphere density and drag with honest error bars
nodes.d: Thermospheric density nowcasts and 1-3 day forecasts with calibrated uncertainty that bring public, operator-usable products from empirical-model spread (20-40% disagreement even in quiet times) to HASDM-class error (about 10-15%) and keep them calibrated through 2-6x storm enhancements…

nodes.t: Predicting when the Sun erupts
nodes.d: Physics-based, probabilistic prediction of flare and CME onset (torus and kink instability thresholds, reconnection onset) from observed active-region magnetic fields, 1-3 days ahead, beating the best operational statistical or ML forecast on an independent benchmark…

nodes.t: Trajectory design on demand
nodes.d: AI agents that take a mission description in plain language and return verified low-thrust, multi-body or low-energy trajectories (ballistic lunar transfers, manifold transfers, gravity-assist tours), with optimality certificates where available, in hours instead of the weeks to months of expert time typical today.

nodes.t: Certified screening that scales to a million objects
nodes.d: Conjunction screening and risk software whose filters are proven never to discard a conjunction above threshold (under stated covariance assumptions), whose code is formally verified, and which is benchmarked to scale to 100,000-1 million objects plus operator ephemerides.

nodes.t: Proven safe capture of tumbling debris
nodes.d: Design and verification tools for capturing objects never meant to be caught: pose and tumble-rate estimation from passive imagery with stated error bounds, approach and synchronization trajectories proven collision-free under that estimation error, detumbling control with guaranteed convergence…

nodes.t: Autonomous Earth-Moon navigation with proven error bounds
nodes.d: Flight demonstration of autonomous cislunar or deep-space navigation (optical, pulsar, lunar GNSS or LunaNet signals) whose filter carries machine-checked integrity bounds.

nodes.t: First large debris object removed from orbit
nodes.d: A servicing spacecraft captures a large non-cooperative object (a spent upper stage or dead satellite) and lowers it to reentry.

nodes.t: Constellations track debris with honest error bars
nodes.d: Star trackers and hosted cameras on at least one megaconstellation (SpaceX Stargaze today) feed conjunction screening used beyond the owner's fleet, by other operators and a government or commercial catalog, with minutes latency and published…

nodes.t: Missions fly AI-designed trajectories
nodes.d: A lunar, cislunar or deep-space mission whose baseline trajectory and contingency set were produced primarily by an AI design agent and verified by the flight-dynamics team.

nodes.t: Radiation-belt and charging risk forecasts days ahead
nodes.d: Probabilistic, physics-consistent forecasts of MeV electron flux and surface/internal charging hazard, 1-3 days ahead for CME-driven enhancements and up to about a week for recurrent high-speed-stream driving…

nodes.t: Missile-tracking satellites cite certified track merging
nodes.d: At a high level: a government proliferated-LEO missile-warning and tracking architecture delivers continuous custody of maneuvering targets by fusing detections across many satellites, and its operators publicly attribute part of the result to fusion and covariance methods of the certified kind…

nodes.t: Storm-proof low-orbit operations
nodes.d: Constellation operators and space-traffic services run conjunction screening and station-keeping on probabilistic density forecasts with realistic covariance, so that at the next G4+ storm the number of objects losing custody and of emergency maneuvers is at least halved versus May 2024.

nodes.t: Autonomous cross-operator collision avoidance
nodes.d: Satellites of at least two large constellation operators (for example Starlink, Amazon Leo, OneWeb; Guowang and Qianfan would need a US-China agreement) detect, negotiate and execute avoidance maneuvers autonomously under a shared protocol with formal safety guarantees…

nodes.t: Traffic management service for Earth-Moon space
nodes.d: An operational catalog, conjunction-screening and coordination service for cislunar space (low lunar orbit, NRHO, DRO, transfers, Earth-Moon L1/L2), comparable to TraCSS for LEO.

nodes.t: Screening-grade catalog of small debris
nodes.d: Tracking data shared with operators that keeps custody of at least 100,000 LEO objects, reaching about 5 cm in the main constellation shells (450-600 km), with covariances good enough for conjunction screening.

nodes.t: Solar-storm arrival forecast within about 8 hours
nodes.d: Operational CME arrival-time forecasts whose best routinely-run ensemble reaches mean absolute error <= 8 h (vs 10.3 h for NASA M2M's Ensemble WSA-Enlil+Cone and 13.2 h across all CCMC scoreboard submissions), with calibrated probability windows.

nodes.t: Commercial constellations below 300 km
nodes.d: At least 100 commercial satellites operating sustainably below 300 km altitude, with propellant and drag margins sized from validated density statistics.

nodes.t: Lunar navigation with proven error bounds in routine use
nodes.d: A lunar navigation service (ESA Moonlight, a LunaNet provider or a commercial relay) broadcasts with integrity monitoring whose protection levels carry machine-checked bounds, and at least three missions, including surface-base operations, use it as a primary navigation source.

nodes.t: Constellation cameras detect debris down to about 2 cm
nodes.d: Dedicated small cameras hosted on at least one megaconstellation detect debris down to about 2 cm at ranges up to a few tens of km, and the detections feed a shared screening catalog.

nodes.t: Side-view and upstream solar-wind monitoring
nodes.d: Operational, guaranteed real-time off-Sun-Earth-line coronagraph and heliospheric imaging (ESA Vigil at L5 with NOAA's CCOR coronagraph) and/or an in-situ monitor well upstream of L1 (sub-L1), giving CME speed, direction and early magnetic-structure data well before arrival…

nodes.t: Knowing a solar storm's magnetic punch a day ahead
nodes.d: Forecasting the southward magnetic field (Bz) of an incoming CME 12-24+ hours before arrival: the main driver of geomagnetic storm severity and of the storm-time density errors that hit satellites.

nodes.t: Debris tracked down to about 2 cm in the busiest shells
nodes.d: A shared, screening-grade catalog keeps custody of most objects larger than about 2 cm that cross the main constellation shells (450-600 km), roughly 50,000-100,000 objects (illustrative: a breakup-model size slope near d^-1.7, and small debris peaks at 750-1,000 km)…

nodes.t: Solar-storm arrival forecast within 6 hours, using Vigil
nodes.d: The best routinely run CME arrival-time forecast reaches a mean absolute error of 6 h or less over at least 40 impacting CMEs, using real-time side-view coronagraph and heliospheric-imager data from ESA's Vigil, with calibrated probability windows.

nodes.t: Debris removal becomes a recurring paid service
nodes.d: At least three defunct satellites or spent stages are removed in one calendar year, at least one of them paid under a commercial contract or a regulatory obligation.

nodes.t: Licensing satellites against an orbital capacity budget
nodes.d: Regulators (FCC, national agencies, eventually ITU) license megaconstellations against an aggregate, model-based orbital capacity or risk budget, using verifiable debris-evolution and conjunction models.

nodes.t: Low Earth orbit stays safe at 100,000 satellites
nodes.d: Collision risk and avoidance-maneuver burden per satellite stop rising, and begin to fall, while the active LEO population grows 3-10x toward 50,000-100,000-plus.

nodes.t: Chinese and Western fleets coordinate maneuvers by machine
nodes.d: At least one Western megaconstellation (for example Starlink) and at least one Chinese megaconstellation (Guowang or Qianfan) exchange ephemerides and maneuver intent machine to machine under an agreed protocol, and resolve close approaches without ad hoc human contact.

nodes.t: Ten or more dead satellites removed in one year
nodes.d: Servicers remove at least 10 defunct satellites or spent stages from orbit in one calendar year, under paid contracts or regulatory obligations.

nodes.t: Landau damping settled for realistic plasmas
nodes.d: Long-time behavior of collisionless and weakly collisional plasmas settled beyond the idealized setting, either by proving nonlinear Landau damping or by proving that it fails.

nodes.t: Relativistic plasma equations proved well-behaved (checked)
nodes.d: The claimed proof that the 3D relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell system has global smooth solutions for smooth finite-energy data passes an outside Comparator run and a statement audit, moving from T3 to T4.

nodes.t: Millisecond fusion-turbulence models trusted in design
nodes.d: Neural and quasilinear surrogates of gyrokinetic turbulence that run in milliseconds, carry calibrated uncertainty, and are trusted inside reactor-design and scenario-planning loops in place of hours-to-weeks nonlinear simulations.

nodes.t: Full-thruster kinetic simulation becomes affordable
nodes.d: AI-designed algorithms (implicit and asymptotic-preserving PIC, low-rank and sparse-grid Vlasov solvers, bounded learned subgrid models) make 3D whole-device kinetic simulation of a Hall thruster with real mass ratio, real geometry and wall physics a days-long rather than infeasible calculation.

nodes.t: A formal library for plasma equations
nodes.d: Agreed, reusable Lean definitions of Vlasov-Poisson/Maxwell, Landau and Boltzmann collision operators, ideal and Hall MHD, and their standard solution concepts, so any claimed result about a plasma model can be audited against a fixed statement.

nodes.t: Plasma simulations with certified error bars
nodes.d: Convergence proofs and computable error bounds for structure-preserving Vlasov-Maxwell, particle-in-cell (PIC) and MHD discretizations, increasingly machine-checked, so code verification can state 'discretization error below X' instead of relying on convergence studies.

nodes.t: Validated models of superconducting magnets
nodes.d: Predictive, validated models for REBCO high-temperature-superconductor coils: quench onset and propagation, screening-current field errors, mechanical strain and delamination, and radiation damage to the conductor, accurate enough to design magnets with smaller margins and fewer full-coil tests.

nodes.t: Simpler plasma models with proven error bounds
nodes.d: Physics theory that derives fluid closures (electron heat flux, anomalous resistivity, pressure anisotropy, Landau-fluid terms) from kinetic theory with stated validity domains and error bounds, replacing ad hoc closures in thruster, magnetic-nozzle and magnetospheric fluid codes.

nodes.t: Solving the 60-year Hall-thruster electron transport puzzle
nodes.d: A validated model of anomalous cross-field electron transport in Hall thrusters, first-principles or data-driven (trained on whole-device kinetic simulations and non-invasive measurements), that predicts transport from the local plasma state across thrusters and operating points without per-condition calibration.

nodes.t: How plasma leaves a magnetic nozzle, settled
nodes.d: Accepted kinetic theory and validated simulation of how plasma detaches from a magnetic nozzle and how electrons cool during the expansion: the thrust-producing stage of VASIMR, helicon thrusters and most fusion-drive concepts.

nodes.t: Nuclear thermal fuel behavior model
nodes.d: A validated multiphysics model of carbide or CERMET fuel corrosion, cracking and fission-product release in 2,500-3,000 K hydrogen under irradiation and thermal cycling.

nodes.t: Deuterium-helium-3 fusion demonstrated at useful rates
nodes.d: Experimental demonstration of significant deuterium-helium-3 fusion power, the fuel most fusion-propulsion concepts assume because only ~5% of its energy comes out as neutrons versus ~80% for D-T (general), at the several-times-higher temperatures it requires.

nodes.t: Nuclear launch safety cases in months
nodes.d: AI produces the reactor design analyses (neutronics, thermal-hydraulics, accident criticality) and the launch-accident nuclear safety analysis needed for NSPM-20 launch authorization of a space fission reactor, cutting a multi-year analysis cycle to months.

nodes.t: AI runs fusion-device experiment campaigns and control
nodes.d: At least one major fusion device (SPARC, Helion Polaris or Orion, W7-X, JT-60SA, DIII-D or KSTAR) runs its main experimental campaign with shots designed in differentiable integrated-modeling codes (e.g. TORAX) and executed under learned controllers (shape, density, heating, disruption avoidance).

nodes.t: AI design loop for stellarator fusion machines
nodes.d: Integrated optimization of stellarator (and other) magnetic configurations against turbulence, fast-ion losses, coil buildability and manufacturing tolerances in weeks, producing designs whose confinement is predicted with error bars.

nodes.t: Design-before-build electric thrusters
nodes.d: Engineering codes that predict a new Hall or gridded-ion thruster's thrust, efficiency, oscillations and plume within a few percent before hardware exists, and extrapolate ground tests to space with quantified uncertainty.

nodes.t: Thruster life proven with shorter wear tests
nodes.d: Erosion and wear models (low-energy sputter yields, pole-cover and cathode-keeper erosion, near-wall plasma) validated well enough that NASA or ESA credits model-based extrapolation for part of the 100% demonstrated-life (wear-test) requirement, not just the margin.

nodes.t: A credible paper design of a fusion rocket
nodes.d: An integrated design of a fusion propulsion system (e.g. Direct Fusion Drive: small field-reversed configuration plus magnetic nozzle, D-He3) whose confinement and nozzle sub-models are validated against experiment, with the D-He3 burn sub-model taken from theory because no device has reached those regimes.

nodes.t: Full-thruster plasma simulation fast enough for design work
nodes.d: Full-device 3D kinetic simulation of a 5 kW-class Hall thruster at real mass ratio, with neutrals and wall emission, runs in hours on a leadership-class machine or in about a day on a commercial cluster.

nodes.t: First magnetic-fusion net energy gain
nodes.d: A magnetic-confinement device reaches scientific gain Q > 1, or Helion delivers net electricity, establishing the energy source that fusion propulsion would ultimately need.

nodes.t: 12 kW Gateway thruster passes a three-year wear test
nodes.d: The AEPS QM-2 thruster completes its long-duration wear test to at least 100% of the PPE mission-based per-thruster xenon throughput requirement (1,770 kg, with the 50% margin shown by analysis under NASA's existing practice).

nodes.t: A U.S. fission reactor launched
nodes.d: The first U.S. space fission reactor since SNAP-10A (1965) is launched: Space Reactor-1 Freedom (nuclear-electric, over 20 kWe) or a Fission Surface Power / Lunar Reactor-1 unit.

nodes.t: Air-breathing electric propulsion flight test
nodes.d: A very-low-orbit satellite that scoops residual atmosphere and uses it as electric-propulsion propellant to cancel drag, demonstrated in orbit.

nodes.t: AI-designed thruster flies and performs as predicted
nodes.d: First in-space operation of an electric thruster whose magnetic circuit, channel and cathode were designed mainly by an AI optimization loop over physics-based (calibrated or kinetic) models, with on-orbit performance inside the pre-flight predicted band and the design attribution published.

nodes.t: 100 kW-class thruster runs for thousands of hours
nodes.d: A >= 100 kW electric thruster (nested Hall, lithium MPD or VASIMR-type) demonstrates >= 5,000 hours of ground operation with validated wear projections toward the ~23,000 hours a crewed Mars nuclear-electric mission needs.

nodes.t: Nuclear thermal engine ground hot fire
nodes.d: A fission-heated hydrogen engine (5-12.5 klbf subscale) fired on the ground with full exhaust capture: the first U.S. NTP reactor test since NERVA (1972).

nodes.t: Fusion-drive ground prototype makes fusion and thrust
nodes.d: A ground prototype built to a closed fusion-propulsion design (plasma-fusion-propulsion-design-closure), using the magnet, heating and nozzle layout of that design at no less than one-tenth of its design heating power, produces measured fusion reactions while exhausting plasma through its magnetic nozzle…

nodes.t: Magnetic radiation shield for crews
nodes.d: A superconducting-magnet active shield demonstrated in space that meaningfully reduces crew dose from solar particle events and galactic cosmic rays at acceptable mass.

nodes.t: Fusion-powered thrust in space
nodes.d: A spacecraft producing mission-useful (newton-class) thrust in orbit from a fusion device operating at or above scientific breakeven, using a low-neutron fuel (in practice D-He3).

nodes.t: A reactor-powered electric spacecraft thrusts for a year
nodes.d: A spacecraft powered by a space fission reactor (Space Reactor-1 Freedom or a successor) runs its electric thrusters on reactor power for a cumulative year in space.

nodes.t: AI-designed thrusters fly across a whole constellation
nodes.d: An electric thruster designed mainly by an AI optimization loop (as defined in plasma-ai-designed-thruster-flight) flies on at least 1,000 satellites of one constellation, with fleet performance inside the pre-flight predicted band and the design attribution public.

nodes.t: Air-breathing electric propulsion in operational service
nodes.d: At least one operational satellite (commercial or government; technology demonstrations do not count) holds a mission orbit below 250 km for at least a year, using air-breathing electric propulsion for drag makeup.

nodes.t: Megawatt electric cargo ships to Mars
nodes.d: An operational nuclear-electric (or megawatt solar-electric) cargo vehicle with MW-class electric propulsion flying to Mars.

nodes.t: Nuclear thermal stage for crewed Mars
nodes.d: A flight-qualified NTP stage (~900 s Isp) available for crewed Mars transits, cutting trip time by up to ~25% (per DOE) and reducing crew radiation dose.

nodes.t: Faster, cheaper electric-propulsion development
nodes.d: Development-to-qualification time for new EP thrusters falls ~15-30% (the base case), up to ~40% (Recursive), and build-test iterations roughly halve because physics-based models replace parts of empirical iteration and, where an agency accepts it, of wear testing.

nodes.t: Humanoid safety standard ISO 25785-1 published
nodes.d: ISO publishes 25785-1, the safety standard for dynamically stable industrial mobile robots (humanoids and other legged or balancing machines).

nodes.t: Robot AI models that work on sites they have never seen
nodes.d: A robot foundation model completes a multi-step task class with at least 90% full-task success on held-out sites it never trained on (factories, warehouses or labs), with results published or audited by a customer.

nodes.t: Proven safety envelopes for robots working beside people
nodes.d: Machine-checked bounds (control barrier functions, reachability sets, runtime monitors) on the behavior of learned whole-body controllers for humanoids or mobile manipulators.

nodes.t: Contact simulation good enough to train robot hands
nodes.d: Policies for contact-rich, multi-finger tasks (fastening, connector mating, cable routing) trained mostly in simulation reach at least 95% success on real hands in production, with under 10% of the training data from the target site.

nodes.t: An accepted route to requalify robot-made flight hardware
nodes.d: A prime contractor, NASA, a NADCAP task group or an AS9100 supplement accepts a documented route for requalifying a special process when general-purpose robots replace human workmanship on flight hardware.

nodes.t: Robot fleets run 1,000 hours between interventions
nodes.d: A maker or operator publishes fleet mean time between interventions (teleoperation, resets or repairs) of at least 1,000 h for a task class, backed by at least 2,300 failure-free robot-hours, the zero-failure demonstration at 90% confidence.

nodes.t: General-purpose robots do multi-task factory work at scale
nodes.d: At least 100,000 general-purpose robots (humanoids and mobile manipulators) do paid, multi-task work in structured factories and warehouses, including robot makers' own lines, at 50% or more of human output per hour and without routine teleoperation.

nodes.t: Precision actuators for 1 million robots a year
nodes.d: World output of precision actuators (planetary roller screws, harmonic or equivalent reducers) is enough to build at least 1 million humanoid-class robots in a year: roughly 14-34 roller screws and about 14 reducers per robot.

nodes.t: One million general-purpose robots in service
nodes.d: The active fleet of general-purpose robots (humanoids and mobile manipulators run by foundation models), counted at year end with a 5-year service life, passes 1 million units.

nodes.t: Robots inspect and refurbish rockets between flights
nodes.d: General-purpose robots do routine post-flight inspection, heat-shield tile handling and replacement, and refurbishment tasks on a reusable heavy launcher at a leading firm, beyond the single-purpose tile and pin machines already in use.

nodes.t: Robots assemble flight hardware at leading space firms
nodes.d: General-purpose robots do paid assembly, integration or test work on flight hardware at aerospace tolerances (torque records, traceability, sub-millimeter fits) at one or more leading space firms, under a requalified process.

nodes.t: Robots run integration and test around the clock
nodes.d: At a leading space firm, robots run a spacecraft or stage integration-and-test line 24/7 (handling, harnessing, mating, test setup and environmental-test loading) with people supervising.

nodes.t: Robots do flight-hardware work across the supplier base
nodes.d: General-purpose robots do requalified flight-hardware work (machining, harnessing, composites, special processes) at 100 or more tier-2 and tier-3 aerospace suppliers.

nodes.t: General-purpose robots do construction trade work at scale
nodes.d: At least 100,000 general-purpose robots do paid construction trade work (electrical, mechanical, framing, finishing) on live sites, beyond material handling and single-task machines.

nodes.t: Robots work in the plants that make robot parts
nodes.d: General-purpose robots do at least 10% of labor hours in reducer, roller-screw, motor or magnet plants of a leading robot supply chain.

nodes.t: Robot crews build a launch pad or propellant plant
nodes.d: A heavy-launch pad or on-site propellant plant (air separation, methane liquefaction, storage) is built with general-purpose robots doing most field trade labor around the clock, in about half the 2026 calendar time.

nodes.t: Robots assemble large structures in orbit at scale
nodes.d: Robots assemble structures larger than any fairing in orbit (100 m class, or radiators and arrays for 100 kW-class and larger platforms) as a repeated commercial operation, beyond one-off demonstrations.

nodes.t: Robots do general lab bench work at scale
nodes.d: At least 50,000 general-purpose robots do the bench work people still do in automated labs (reagent prep, plate loading, instrument tending, moving samples between workcells), so leading autonomous labs run without human hands in the loop.

nodes.t: Robots build lunar pads, berms and roads at outpost scale
nodes.d: Multi-task robots build and maintain lunar surface infrastructure at outpost scale: at least two landing pads sized for heavy landers, plus blast berms and roads, about 10,000 m2 of prepared surface in all, kept in use over six or more lunar days.

nodes.t: Robots supply a quarter of aerospace production labor
nodes.d: General-purpose robots supply productive labor equal to 25% of the ~2 million-person global aerospace production workforce of 2026.

nodes.t: Robots work in the plants that make heavy equipment
nodes.d: General-purpose robots do at least 10% of labor hours in plants that make large power transformers, cryogenic and compressor plant, or machine tools, in at least one leading economy.

nodes.t: Ten million general-purpose robots in service
nodes.d: The active general-purpose robot fleet passes 10 million units, about twice today's stock of industrial robots.

nodes.t: Robots supply 10% of global manufacturing labor
nodes.d: General-purpose robots supply productive labor equal to 10% of the ~460 million-person global manufacturing workforce of 2026, counted as human-equivalents (robot hours x productivity x productive share of the fleet).
